explain.say: Casting means pouring liquid metal into a hollow shape and letting it set. Sand casting starts with a pattern, a copy of the part made in wood, plastic or metal.

explain.say: Special sand mixed with clay is rammed tightly around the pattern in a two-part box. When the box is opened and the pattern lifted out, it leaves a hollow the exact shape of the part.

explain.say: The box is closed and molten metal is poured into a channel called the sprue until it fills the hollow. Extra reservoirs called risers hold spare metal to feed the part as it shrinks.

faq.a: A pattern is a model of the part, used to make the hollow in the sand. It is made slightly oversize to allow for shrinking, with gently sloping sides so it can be pulled out without damaging the mould.
asks: Why is a pattern used in casting?

faq.q: Why is sand used for moulds?
faq.a: Sand can survive the heat of molten metal, it packs into fine detail when mixed with a little clay, it lets gases escape, and it can be broken away and reused. It is also cheap.
asks: Why don't foundries use metal moulds?

faq.q: What are the sprue and risers for?
faq.a: The sprue is the channel the metal is poured into, leading to the hollow. Risers are extra pockets of molten metal that stay liquid longest and feed the part as it shrinks, so it has no holes.

faq.q: Why is a casting pattern made bigger than the part?
faq.a: Metals shrink as they cool from liquid to room temperature, by about 1 to 2 percent for many. Making the pattern that much bigger means the finished casting comes out the right size.
asks: Why does metal shrink when it cools?

faq.q: What things are made by sand casting?
faq.a: Car engine blocks, pump bodies, manhole covers, large machine bases and bells are often sand cast, because it can make big, complicated shapes cheaply.

facts: Metal casting is one of the oldest manufacturing methods; copper objects were being cast more than 5,000 years ago.
Many car engine blocks are sand cast in iron or aluminium.
